history.heading: Turtles and seafarers
paragraphs: The Cayman Islands, three low islands south of Cuba (Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman), were uninhabited when Christopher Columbus sighted them in 1503. He named them Las Tortugas after the many sea turtles, which later attracted ships seeking fresh meat.

Permanent settlement began in the 18th century, with settlers, enslaved Africans, shipwrecked sailors and others. The islands were governed as a dependency of Jamaica. For generations Caymanian men worked as seamen and turtle fishermen.

history.heading: Modern development
paragraphs: When Jamaica became independent in 1962, the Cayman Islands chose to remain a British dependency. From the 1960s the territory developed as a financial centre and tourist destination, transforming a modest seafaring community into one of the richest places in the Caribbean. Hurricane Ivan caused heavy damage in 2004.

culture.heading: Island life
paragraphs: English is the official language. Caymanians blend British, African and Caribbean traditions, and a large share of residents are expatriates working in finance and tourism. Most people are Christian, and Sunday is widely observed.
Turtle stew and conch are traditional dishes. Pirates Week festival celebrates the islands' seafaring past, and Seven Mile Beach and Stingray City are famous attractions.

politics.heading: British Overseas Territory
paragraphs: The Cayman Islands are a British Overseas Territory. An elected Parliament and a premier handle most domestic matters, while a governor appointed by the British monarch is responsible for defence, foreign affairs, internal security and the police.

economy.heading: Global financial centre
paragraphs: The Cayman Islands are one of the world's largest offshore financial centres, especially for hedge funds, investment funds and insurance. There is no income, corporate or capital gains tax; revenue comes from fees and import duties. This has drawn international criticism, and the territory has adopted transparency rules.
Tourism, including cruise ships, is the second pillar. The Cayman Islands dollar is pegged to the US dollar, and incomes and living costs are very high.
